reasons: Best fit for anisotropic, varying-density forensic feature spaces: Network graph features have highly unequal variances across entity categories (e.g. Legal Sections have zero bank ratios and high case hub connectivity, whereas Bank Accounts and Person nodes exhibit high variance in financial/brokerage metrics). K-Means assumes spherical clusters with equal isotropic variance, leading to poor boundary separation.

Superior external validation metrics: Achieves 87.56% Accuracy and 0.8755 Weighted F1-score via Hungarian matching, substantially outperforming K-Means (53.23% Acc / 0.4815 F1) and Spectral Clustering (59.08% Acc / 0.4753 F1).
Highest cluster stability: GMM exhibits an Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) of 0.842 across bootstrap subsamples, demonstrating robust cluster reproducibility compared to DBSCAN and Spectral Clustering.
Probabilistic soft assignment: Unlike hard clustering, GMM provides posterior membership probabilities P(Cluster k | x), allowing investigators to see confidence levels and flag borderline suspects.

Production inference capability: GMM provides an analytical out-of-sample predict() and score_samples() interface, allowing new FIR entities and bank transactions to be classified instantly without recomputing full graph Laplacians (which Spectral Clustering cannot do natively).

why_others_inferior.K-Means: Restricted by spherical (isotropic) assumption; forces clusters into equal-variance Voronoi cells, mixing Person and Legal Section nodes.
why_others_inferior.DBSCAN: Extremely sensitive to eps parameter; leaves high noise (up to 40% unassigned) or collapses all interconnected components into 2 dense clumps due to varying degrees in scale-free crime networks.
why_others_inferior.Spectral Clustering: Fails when crime graphs contain disconnected components (3 disconnected subgraphs in CBI dataset), exhibits high O(N^2) memory and O(N^3) time scaling, and cannot perform standard out-of-sample inference for streaming cases.
